summary: This memo describes the US top-level domains of the early Internet, which placed US organisations under the .us space using geographic names such as states and localities. It was informational and was replaced by RFC 1480.

eli5.summary: Every country gets its own ending for web names, and this paper explains how the United States organised the names that end in .us. A newer paper later replaced it.

subtitle: How the United States domain space is organized by geography

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a country domain for the United States, and had to decide how to organize the names under it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1386 establishes the .US domain as a top-level country domain organized by political geography: state, then city, then organization, allowing every US computer to be registered without conflicts.
tldr.outcome: The .US domain provides a geographic naming structure for government agencies, schools, libraries, and other organizations nationwide. RFC 1480 later updated it.

today: RFC 1480 updated and replaced RFC 1386 as the specification for the .US domain.

sections.title: The DNS and Country Domains
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) translates human-readable names like venera.isi.edu to IP addresses. Most early Internet organizations registered under the generic top-level domains: EDU (education), COM (commercial), GOV (government), MIL (military), ORG (organizations), NET (networks), and INT (international). However, every country also has a two-letter country code from ISO-3166 (for example, UK for United Kingdom, FR for France).

The US Domain is the official country domain for the United States, established as a top-level domain using the ISO code US. Unlike EDU and COM (which are used worldwide), the US domain is reserved for entities in the United States and uses a geographic organization structure. The domain is administered by Jon Postel and Ann Westine Cooper at USC-ISI.
sections.eli5: DNS lets you type names instead of numbers to reach computers. Countries have domain endings like .uk. The United States has .us, which is organized like a mailing address: state, city, then organization.

sections.title: The Geographic Hierarchy
sections.content:
The US Domain hierarchy mirrors political geography: the first level is the two-letter state abbreviation (like CA for California, NY for New York), the second level is the city or locality (like LosAngeles or San-Francisco), and the third level is the organization or computer name. For example: Zuckys.Santa-Monica.CA.US represents a restaurant named Zuckys in Santa Monica, California.

City names can be spelled out in full with hyphens replacing spaces (San-Francisco, Los-Angeles), or use abbreviations from Western Union's City Mnemonics list, or custom abbreviations. Once a city code is established, all registrations in that city must use the same code for consistency. For large organizations with multiple facilities, the headquarters location is used. Additionally, delegated subdomains exist for specialized categories: K12 for kindergarten through 12th grade schools, CC for community colleges, LIB for libraries, STATE for state government agencies, and FED for federal agencies.
sections.eli5: The structure is like a postal address: state code (two letters), city name (full or abbreviated), then the organization. For example, a school might be under k12.ca.us (kindergarten-12 in California). Government agencies go under state.ca.us or fed.us.

sections.title: How Registration Works
sections.content:
Anyone registering a host in the US Domain must fill out a US Domain questionnaire and follow the domain's policies. The registrant must provide an administrative contact and a technical contact, both with valid working email addresses. Key contacts must have Internet-style email addresses (not UUCP-style addresses like host1!user). For UUCP hosts (computers reachable through the UUCP network), an Internet forwarder is required to act as a mail relay. For non-IP hosts, the DNS entry contains an MX (mail exchange) record pointing to an Internet host that relays mail.

Registration can be done directly with the US Domain administrator (us-domain@isi.edu) or through Internet service providers that have established relationships with the administrator. Turnround time is typically one or two days, and nameservers are updated within 12 to 24 hours.

The registrar also manages withdrawal of records by receiving a revised record with a higher revision number and withdrawal notes, and handles UUCP sites that feed into a central site without requiring individual registration for each downstream site.
sections.eli5: To register a computer in .us, you fill out a form with admin and tech contact information and send it to the US Domain office. If your computer is on UUCP (an older network protocol), you need an Internet computer to forward your mail. Registration takes a day or two.

sections.title: Delegated Subdomains and Administration
sections.content:
The administrator of the US Domain cannot manage all registrations alone, so portions of the namespace are delegated to others. Delegated zones include city domains (like SF.CA.US), state subdomains (STATE.MN.US for Minnesota government), federal domains (FED.US for federal agencies), and school/library/college subdomains. Currently, about 680 individual hosts are directly registered, with additional hosts registered under delegated subdomains.

To receive delegation, the applicant must demonstrate technical expertise with DNS, provide at least two independent nameservers in separate locations, accept all applicants equally, and provide timely processing. When a subdomain is delegated, the delegated administrator receives the current zone file and registers their nameservers with the US Domain. Wildcard records are allowed under organizational subdomains but not under city or state domains.

The RFC lists about 35 delegated zones with their technical contacts, including zones for cities (SF.CA.US, Denver.CO.US), schools (K12.CA.US, CC.CA.US), state government (STATE.MN.US), and federal agencies (MNPL.FRB.FED.US).
sections.eli5: Delegating means giving control of a part of the domain to someone else. For example, someone runs the.sf.ca.us domain for San Francisco, or state.ca.us for California government. The delegate must have two independent nameservers and process requests fairly.

sections.title: DNS Records and Zone Management
sections.content:
The US Domain uses standard DNS resource records: A records map hostnames to IP addresses, CNAME records create aliases (useful when an organization moves and creates a pointer from the old name to the new location), MX records designate mail exchange servers for non-IP hosts, HINFO records describe host hardware and operating system, and PTR records support reverse DNS lookup.

Zone files contain nameserver (NS) records listing the authoritative servers for each zone. The RFC examples show zone files with SOA (start of authority) records defining zone parameters like serial number, refresh interval, and retry values. Nameservers are listed with their IP addresses as glue records when necessary (when the nameserver's hostname is itself within the delegated domain).
sections.eli5: The DNS database uses standard record types: A maps a name to an IP address, CNAME creates an alias, MX sends mail to the right server. Zone files list which servers manage which domains.
